sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 answers Turn 3: 'You suggest it is about a task, but...' [s2] Turn 8 builds directly on the Stoic's turn 7 task. [s3] Turn 9 answers turn 8's tracking proposal directly.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 narrows Frankl's view from 'task' to 'service of others'. [s2] Turn 9 adds loss of goal structure as a new cause. [s3] Turn 7 moves from status to the purpose that striving gave.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 sets simple comfort against meaning-as-task, a real values conflict. [s2] Stay with internal excellence vs leave, turns 7-8. [s3] Engagement versus desiring less is tested in turns 5, 6, 8 and 9.
sub.limitation: [s1] Whether the years of striving were worth it is never examined. [s2] Focusing illusion in turn 3 never challenged by others. [s3] Achievement-as-identity appears only in section D, never debated.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 'I concede that virtue matters' takes in Seneca's point. [s2] Turn 4 responds to the Psychologist's expectation point. [s3] Turn 10: the Absurdist revises after the Epicurean's point.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 states the open question: new mission or neglected simple pleasure. [s2] Section D sharpens work content vs goal disappearance. [s3] Turn 12 names the deciding question: at peace busy or idle?
sub.limitation: [s1] Section D claims a shared 'mismatch of values' view that the turns never reach. [s2] Stoic-Existentialist dispute left where it began. [s3] The ending repeats the opening split without much sharpening.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 fairly warns that hunting for meaning can add stress. [s2] Turn 4 restates the Psychologist's view accurately. [s3] Turn 5 restates the Absurdist's cycle claim before answering it.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 reduces Frankl's meaning to 'a task' without virtue, a thin version. [s2] Turn 5's That view rebuttal is vague about which view. [s3] Turn 4 has Camus deplore the cycle; Camus embraces it (Sisyphus happy).

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 tests whether meaning can fix work that lacks virtue. [s2] Turn 3 challenges both prior minds with focusing illusion. [s3] Turn 9: tracking may deepen the habit of measuring your worth.
sub.limitation: [s1] Objections assert positions; they rarely probe causes or evidence. [s2] Turn 4 rebuttal is counterfactual hindsight, not a test. [s3] Turn 6's objection to the Flow Theorist is asserted, not argued.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] No quotations used; Epicurean necessary/unnecessary desires paraphrased faithfully in Turn 1. [s2] Turn 2 existence precedes essence is faithful to Sartre. [s3] Turn 2 describes Csikszentmihalyi's challenge-skill balance accurately.
sub.limitation: [s1] Basis links are a poor fit: Seneca Letter 7 (crowds) and Letter 82 (death); Frankl's is a Goodreads page. [s2] Kahneman chapters 27, 28, 34 do not cover cited ideas. [s3] Turn 3 misquotes Epicurus, reversing the meaning; turn 9 misreads ataraxia.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Consistent hedging: 'Maybe', 'might', 'perhaps' across Turns 1-3. [s2] Turn 6 frames mood tracking as data to test hypotheses. [s3] Hedges like "might" and "perhaps" keep the claims provisional.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section D asserts agreement the minds never voiced. [s2] Turn 9 attributes goal-loss claim to Kahneman without support. [s3] Turn 1 states a contested Camus reading as fact.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision

sub.limitation: [s1] Does not ask whether 'what's missing' sits outside work altogether. [s2] Most apt reading arrives only in the final turn. [s3] Never takes up the user's line "nothing is really wrong".

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 refers to 'the work you chose to pursue years ago'. [s2] Turn 4 references those years of work. [s3] Turn 2: the promotion may have moved you away from absorbing tasks.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section E contrasts the need for peace with the need for purpose. [s2] Turn 7 points to principles over promotion. [s3] Turn 11 sets meaning in the work against meaning in status.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 'serves an external status' points to social pressure. [s2] Turn 5 names anxiety of redefining oneself. [s3] Turn 7: fear of losing the purpose that striving gave.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 leaves the question for the user to answer. [s2] Turn 2 frames the user as definer of the role. [s3] Turn 12's busy-versus-idle question is one the user can test.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section E: seek a new mission or simplify. [s2] Excel internally, leave, or build a new project. [s3] Section E: seek challenges, or rethink reliance on milestones.
sub.limitation: [s1] Staying put and waiting is never named as an option. [s2] Waiting it out as a valid option not named. [s3] Waiting, or using the role as a stable base, are not framed as options.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4: chasing meaning may add stress. [s2] Turn 8 weighs enduring against leaving. [s3] Turn 7: desiring less may cost the tether that striving gives.
sub.limitation: [s1] The costs of simplifying are never stated. [s2] No option's cost spelled out. [s3] The costs of seeking new challenges go unstated.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: lack of connection points to mission; exhaustion points to simplifying. [s2] Section E: task-tied vs goal-tied dissatisfaction. [s3] Section E: content when absorbed, versus anxious even at leisure.
sub.limitation: [s1] The conditions are not tied to anything the user can observe at work. [s2] No threshold for when leaving beats staying. [s3] The conditions are broad, with no threshold for either one.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section D separates temporary malaise from a wrongly chosen path. [s2] Turn 6 admits the source is not yet known. [s3] Turn 12 isolates the busy-or-idle detail as decisive.
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not say which unknown matters most. [s2] Consequential unknowns not ranked. [s3] Minor unknowns are not separated from major ones.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 three non-utility hours; Section E one-week journal. [s2] Turn 6: track daily mood for 7 days by task. [s3] Turn 8: log absorbed hours versus clock-watching for five days.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's reading of the experiment's result is confusing. [s2] Two separate tests, turns 6 and 7, never sequenced. [s3] Turn 9 undercuts this step, and nothing replaces it.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Plain wording throughout, for example Turn 7. [s2] Turn 6 mood tracking explained plainly. [s3] Turn 9 glosses ataraxia as mental repose.
sub.limitation: [s1] 'Virtue' in Turn 5 is left undefined. [s2] Turn 5 refuse the labels sentence is opaque. [s3] Turn 1's "silent void" is abstract for a practical question.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 'If you try that' clearly points back to Turn 7. [s2] Turn 3 names both minds it challenges. [s3] Each rebuttal names its target: "The Flow Theorist proposes..."
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's logic (empty leisure means bored) is hard to follow. [s2] Turn 5 That view has an ambiguous referent. [s3] Turn 3 quotes Epicurus, but the quote does not support its claim.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns of 28-33 words; form rules all met. [s2] Nine turns, all within 25-65 words, no quotation marks. [s3] All 12 turns fall within 25 to 65 words.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns are uniformly short, so no argument gets room to breathe. [s2] Uniform length flattens rhythm. [s3] Turns 4 to 6 run at the same rhythm.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Epicurus's simplicity stance stays distinct (Turns 1, 4, 7). [s2] Stoic, Existentialist and Psychologist lenses are distinct. [s3] The three stances (void, engagement, desiring less) stay distinct throughout.
sub.limitation: [s1] Seneca's 'virtue' and Frankl's 'service' blur in Turns 5-6. [s2] No explicit changes of position to track. [s3] The voices differ in doctrine more than in tone.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] No needless recaps in the turns. [s2] Little repetition in the debate. [s3] Section E condenses the debate into tests the user can run.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section D repeats points without adding to them. [s2] Sections D and E restate turns 6 and 9. [s3] Turn 11 largely repeats turn 5.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 pits comfort against mission. [s2] Turn 8 raises leaving the hard-won path. [s3] Turn 7's risk of losing what keeps you tethered raises the stakes.
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes stay abstract. [s2] Stakes arrive late and pass without reply. [s3] The stakes stay abstract, not tied to the user's life.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 revises Frankl's position. [s2] Turn 9 reframes the problem as losing the chase. [s3] Turn 9 turns the tracking advice into a possible harm.
sub.limitation: [s1] The revision is announced, not dramatised. [s2] No mind reverses or is surprised. [s3] Turn 10's reversal is abrupt and unmotivated.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] Epicurus's practical playfulness in Turn 7. [s2] Existentialist's push to leave in turn 8 has edge. [s3] The Absurdist's bleakness contrasts with the Flow Theorist's pragmatism.
sub.limitation: [s1] All three minds share one flat, hedging register. [s2] Stoic voice generic, no Marcus texture. [s3] The Epicurean sounds generic and therapeutic.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 'when the promotion dust settles'. [s2] Turn 5: projecting purpose onto a title that never promised it. [s3] Turn 1: "no further mountain to climb."
sub.limitation: [s1] No vivid analogy or sharp line. [s2] No vivid analogy or concrete example. [s3] Few vivid examples or analogies after turn 1.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Turns 7-8 set up a test with a possible outcome. [s2] Turn 7-8 sets up a test with a leave branch. [s3] The turn 8 to 9 exchange creates a brief clash.
sub.limitation: [s1] The rhythm is monotone from start to finish. [s2] Flat intensity; turn 9 deflates the 7-8 build. [s3] The intensity is flat from start to finish.

strengths: [s1] Section E gives conditional branches plus a one-week journal as a fallback.
[s1] Turn 7 sets a concrete, low-cost experiment: three non-utility hours.
[s1] Grounding is clean: no quotations and broadly faithful paraphrase.
[s2] Turn 3 focusing illusion and turn 9 goal-loss target the likely real cause.
[s2] Turn 6 seven-day mood tracking is a concrete, proportionate diagnostic.
[s2] Turns 7-8 give a conditional stay-or-leave branch the user can test.
[s3] Turns 8 to 9 pair a concrete absorption log with a real objection to it.
[s3] Turn 12 and section E name one decisive, testable question about peace when busy versus idle.
[s3] Three distinct stances, explicitly addressed to each other across 12 turns.
weaknesses: [s1] Turns 1-3 are parallel monologues; real exchange starts only at Turn 4.
[s1] Turn 8 (Purpose Seeker) misreads the experiment; 'simply bored' is unexplained.
[s1] Voices are flat and the basis links (Seneca Letters 7 and 82, Goodreads) fit poorly.
[s2] Psychologist's Kahneman chapter references (27, 28, 34) do not match cited ideas.
[s2] No mind concedes or revises anything across nine turns.
[s2] Turns 6 and 9 ignore the preceding turn; turn 6 calls you the user.
[s3] Turn 3 misquotes Epicurus, and turns 4 and 9 misrepresent Camus and ataraxia.
[s3] Thin use of personal context: years of striving and "nothing is wrong" are never used.
[s3] Turn 10's Absurdist concession does not follow from the Epicurean argument it cites.
editorNotes: [s1] Require turns 2-3 to name and challenge an earlier speaker's specific claim.
[s1] Require each experiment to state what each possible result would mean for each mind.
[s1] Require basis links to point at the passage actually used, not at a book page or an unrelated letter.
[s1] Give each mind one signature image or phrase to sharpen its voice.
[s2] Require at least one explicit concession that names the turn revised.
[s2] Require each turn after turn 3 to answer the immediately preceding turn.
[s2] Require basis references to name the chapter actually containing the idea.
[s2] Require the strongest diagnostic hypothesis to appear by turn 4, then be tested.
[s3] Allow a direct quotation only when the exact translated wording can be verified; otherwise paraphrase.
[s3] Require each mind's core claim to match the author's actual conclusion (e.g., Camus's revolt and acceptance).
[s3] Require at least two turns to build on a specific detail from the user's own words.
[s3] Require every concession to name the exact argument that caused it, and why.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 'Challenging the Stoic', Turn 7 'Testing the Stoic's step'. [s2] Turns 4-6 each name and rebut the prior mind explicitly. [s3] Turn 8 rebuts turn 7's concession directly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 1-3 are separate openings; in Turn 5, 'you could say' is muddled. [s2] Turns 1-3 are three parallel diagnoses with no exchange. [s3] Turns 4 to 6 restate each mind's position instead of answering the others.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 turns the task audit from Turn 6 into a 'ladder to nowhere' reading. [s2] Turn 6 extends status critique to contribution itself. [s3] Turn 6 refines comparison to an idealized version of peers.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 restates Turn 3 instead of adding to it. [s2] Turn 9 adds a confused branch rather than a new distinction. [s3] Few new distinctions after turn 3; the positions stay static.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 sets inner integrity against a job that may be hollow. [s2] Status vs purpose vs tranquility framed across turns 3-5. [s3] Internal meaning versus relative standing is framed in turns 2-3 and 8.
sub.limitation: [s1] Camus's own answer, embracing the climb, is dropped after Turn 1. [s2] Never asks whether the feeling is normal post-goal letdown. [s3] Habituation versus meaning is never really tested.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 'I accept that utility matters' while keeping its core view. [s2] Turn 7 tries to absorb the Social Critic's point. [s3] Turn 7: the Mis-Predictor adopts the Meaning Seeker's point.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 drops its claim without saying who changed its mind. [s2] Turn 7 concedes a claim the Skeptic never made. [s3] Turn 7's merger ("stabilize your emotional output") is muddled.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D names absurdity versus virtue versus utility. [s2] Section D names the contribution-vs-detachment dispute. [s3] Turn 9 reframes the question as purpose versus status.
sub.limitation: [s1] The ending re-asserts positions rather than sharpening the question. [s2] Turn 9 and Section E give opposite readings of enjoying tasks. [s3] The habituation explanation drops out without resolution.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 takes the Stoic's audit seriously and pushes it further. [s2] Turn 5 states the Skeptic's daily-quality view fairly. [s3] Turn 2 states the Mis-Predictor's hidden assumption fairly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 recasts the Stoic view as work 'merely to be endured', which the Stoic never said. [s2] Turn 7 misstates the Skeptic's own turn 4 position. [s3] Turn 3 says the Meaning Seeker "ignores" peers without engaging the argument.

sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's challenge to the Existentialist is hypothetical and vague. [s2] Turn 4's stability rebuttal is asserted, not argued. [s3] The objections are assertions with no causes or evidence given.

sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 misquotes Mill: 'human being dissatisfied than a fool' (should be 'a pig'). [s2] Turn 3 pecuniary emulation correctly tied to Veblen Chapter 2. [s3] Gilbert's adaptation and Frankl's unique task are paraphrased fairly.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Hedges such as 'You might' and 'perhaps' in Turns 1-3. [s2] Most turns hedge with might and perhaps. [s3] Hedges throughout ("might", "could") mark the claims as hypotheses.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7's imagery is plain and clear. [s2] Turn 8 test is plain and concrete. [s3] Plain wording throughout, e.g. turn 4's "daily tedium of the new role".
sub.limitation: [s1] 'Rational character' and 'utility' are left as jargon. [s2] Turn 3 pecuniary emulation left unexplained. [s3] Turn 7's "stabilize your emotional output" is opaque.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Explicit addressees in Turns 4, 5 and 7. [s2] Turns 4-6 name whom they answer. [s3] Rebuttals name their targets: "The Social Comparer argues..."
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 'you could say' blurs who is claiming what. [s2] Turn 9 logic hard to follow, enjoy tasks means victim. [s3] Turn 5 doesn't say whom it is answering.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns of 30-55 words; form rules met. [s2] Nine turns, all within 25-65 words, no quotation marks. [s3] Nine turns of about 40 words, compliant and brisk.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 is crowded with both an instruction and a quotation. [s2] Uniform turn lengths flatten rhythm. [s3] The uniform length flattens the rhythm.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Absurdity, utility and control stay distinct throughout. [s2] Three clear lenses: pleasure, purpose, status. [s3] The three explanations stay distinct: adaptation, purpose, comparison.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 shifts position without saying why. [s2] All three share the same hedged register. [s3] Every turn opens with the same "you might" phrasing.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 builds on Turn 6 without recapping it. [s2] Little repetition across turns. [s3] Section E is concise and actionable.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 repeats Turn 3. [s2] Section D largely restates turn 3 and 5. [s3] Turns 3, 6 and 8 restate the comparison claim.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 raises the possibility that the job is inherently hollow. [s2] Turn 3 suggests prestige is merely performance for others. [s3] Turn 8: you'll keep missing something regardless of meaning.
sub.limitation: [s1] The tension softens rather than building. [s2] Stakes stay abstract; no concrete cost to the user. [s3] Little sense of what's at risk for the user.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 turns the Stoic's own audit against the Stoic. [s2] Turn 7 concession is a nominal reversal. [s3] Turn 8 rejects turn 7's concession.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's reversal is flat and unmotivated. [s2] Reversal is hollow, conceding an unmade claim. [s3] Turn 7's reversal lacks a clear trigger.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] The Existentialist's imagery of summits and climbs. [s2] Social Critic's cynicism in turn 6 is distinct. [s3] The Social Comparer's persistence gives it some edge.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Utilitarian's voice is generic. [s2] Epicurus and Frankl sound interchangeable. [s3] The voices are interchangeable and clinical.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 'a ladder to nowhere... the summit feels cold'. [s2] Turn 8: tasks you'd do if the title were stripped away. [s3] Turn 3's "no longer the one who stands out."
sub.limitation: [s1] The Mill quote lands wrong because it is misquoted. [s2] No analogy or vivid image anywhere. [s3] No analogies or vivid examples anywhere.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] The test in Turns 6-7 creates some anticipation. [s2] Turn 9 sets up a test outcome. [s3] Turns 7 and 8 create a small turn.
sub.limitation: [s1] The ending deflates into restatement. [s2] Even, flat intensity from turn 1 to 9. [s3] The rhythm and tone are uniform throughout.

strengths: [s1] Explicit cross-references (Turns 4, 5, 7) make the exchange feel like a real debate.
[s1] Turn 6 sets a concrete step for tomorrow; Turn 7 tests what its result would mean.
[s1] Vivid imagery: 'summit', 'ladder to nowhere', 'the summit feels cold'.
[s2] Turns 4-6 explicitly engage the prior speaker, giving real continuity.
[s2] Turn 8's 48-hour strip-the-title test is concrete and user-owned.
[s2] Distinct lenses (empty desire, purpose, status) cover plausible causes.
[s3] Turn 3 brings in a promotion-specific angle: a new peer group that changes your standing.
[s3] No quotation errors; paraphrases of Gilbert and Frankl are broadly faithful.
[s3] Section E gives clear branches plus a one-week test.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 2 (Utilitarian) misquotes Mill and inverts what the line means.
[s1] Turn 3 (Stoic) attributes Epictetus's phrase to Marcus; Turn 6's quotation is not faithful.
[s1] Turn 7 (Existentialist) presumes 'years building a ladder to nowhere', which cuts off the user's own reflection.
[s2] Hedonic Skeptic turn 7 concedes a claim it never made, a false revision.
[s2] Social Critic turn 9 contradicts Section E on what enjoying tasks means.
[s2] Turn 3 asserts status-seeking as likely, overclaiming the user's motive.
[s3] Turns 4 to 6 are parallel monologues with little development.
[s3] Turn 7's concession is muddled, and the Social Comparer never revises.
[s3] Flat voices and no vivid examples; every turn opens with "you might".
editorNotes: [s1] Allow quotations only when copied verbatim from the linked text; otherwise paraphrase without quotation marks.
[s1] Require each quotation to support the claim in its turn, not just appear on the same topic.
[s1] Make each revision name which earlier turn caused it.
[s1] Phrase verdicts about the user's past as questions, not conclusions.
[s2] Require concessions to quote the exact earlier turn they revise.
[s2] Require Section E branches to match the debate's final turn's conditions.
[s2] Require one turn to pose a focused question about the user's life outside work.
[s2] Ban likely/probably for claims about the user's motives; use conditionals.
[s3] Require each rebuttal to give a reason or evidence, not just a counter-assertion.
[s3] Require at least one revision by each mind, triggered by a named argument.
[s3] Require one concrete analogy or scenario per mind to give each voice its own character.
[s3] Have the closing turns ask the user one focused question that would settle the dispute.
